prompt: Why does this lesson ask about price last rather than first?
hint: Think of Athena's 9.00 a terabyte and the "my orders" screen.

choices.text: Because price is the least important of the six
choices.why: It matters a great deal; it just cannot be read before the workload says what to multiply.

choices.text: A price means something only once the workload says what to multiply
choices.why: Right. Read first, Athena's per-terabyte price would have ruled in a store the access pattern rules out.

choices.text: Because the price sheet only covers some stores
choices.why: It covers every store of this lesson; the order is about reasoning, not data.

choices.text: Because managed services all cost about the same
choices.why: The worked comparison found 10.50 against 338.25 for one workload.

prompt: Put the six questions in the order this lesson asks them.
hint: The shape of the work first, the bill last.
items: How fast must an answer come?
What consistency does the reader need?
How big, and how fast does it grow?
What does it cost, at this workload?

prompt: At checkout, Quitanda shows a loyalty balance that must include the points the customer earned a second ago in the same purchase. Which question rules out answering it from a cache or from the warehouse?
hint: Both of those are, by design, behind the source.

choices.text: Latency, since a warehouse answers in seconds
choices.why: True of the warehouse, and a cache answers in under a millisecond; what excludes both is that neither sees the write just made.

choices.text: Scale, since loyalty grows with every purchase
choices.why: The data is small; size is not what fails here.

choices.text: Consistency
choices.why: Right: the reader must see the latest write, which the store of record gives and its copies do not.

choices.text: Price, since a cache costs money every hour
choices.why: Price comes last and is not what disqualifies them.

prompt: A team of three runs Aurora and S3 well. A new feature needs a small lookup by key, about 50 requests a second, next to data that is already in Aurora. Which question argues most for keeping it in Aurora rather than adding DynamoDB?
hint: Count the stores the team runs.

choices.text: Scale: DynamoDB cannot serve as few as 50 requests a second
choices.why: It serves any rate; small loads are not a problem for it.

choices.text: Who operates it: one store fewer to run
choices.why: Right. At 50 a second an indexed query is easy for Aurora, and the team avoids a new store to learn and watch.

choices.text: Price: Aurora is cheaper per request than DynamoDB in every case
choices.why: The worked comparison found the opposite for a workload alone; Aurora wins here because it is already paid for.

choices.text: Consistency: DynamoDB offers no strong reads
choices.why: It offers strongly consistent reads per request.

prompt: Match each workload to the branch of the tree it belongs on.
hint: Ask the first question of each.

pairs.left: a cart read and written by the customer's id many times a minute
contracts kept for seven years and read almost never
an order, its lines and the stock, all or nothing
a dashboard refreshed all day by forty analysts

right_distractors: ElastiCache, as the store of record

prompt: Why is ElastiCache never the store of record in this lesson's designs?
hint: What happens to its data when a node restarts?

choices.text: It is too slow for writes
choices.why: It is the fastest store of the course.

choices.text: It keeps data only until eviction or a restart
choices.why: Right, which makes it a copy in front of a store that keeps the data for good.

choices.text: It costs more per GB than any database
choices.why: Memory is dear, and that is not why it cannot be the record.

choices.text: It cannot be read by more than one application
choices.why: Any number of clients read a cache.

prompt: A fraud check needs the orders placed in the last minute. The analyst writes it against Redshift, which is loaded every hour. What is wrong?
hint: Which store knows about the last minute?

choices.text: Redshift cannot filter on time
choices.why: It filters on time very well, over the data it has.

choices.text: The query needs a sort key on the order date
choices.why: A sort key makes it faster over loaded data; the last minute is not loaded yet.

choices.text: Redshift answers as of the last load, and "now" lives in the store of record or the stream
choices.why: Right: Aurora or the Kinesis stream knows the last minute; the warehouse learns it within the hour.

choices.text: Fraud checks must run on Athena
choices.why: Athena reads the lake, which is behind the source too.

prompt: Carts would work in Aurora. Why does Quitanda put them in DynamoDB?
hint: Access by one key, spikes, and abandoned carts.

choices.text: One key, spiky load, and expiry deleting abandoned carts for free
choices.why: Right, and the business database stays free of rows nobody keeps.

choices.text: Aurora cannot store a cart's list of products
choices.why: A table of cart lines does that easily.

choices.text: A cart must be joined to the stock on every read
choices.why: If it did, that would argue for Aurora; nothing joins it until it becomes an order.

choices.text: DynamoDB is the store of record for orders
choices.why: Orders live in Aurora; a cart is copied there when it becomes one.

prompt: A dashboard runs 300 queries a day on Athena, each scanning 20 GB, at 9.00 USD a terabyte. What does it cost a day, in USD?
hint: 20 GB is 0.02 TB.

prompt: Each dashboard query scans 20 GB, 0.18 USD on Athena. A Redshift Serverless workgroup at 8 RPUs, busy ten hours, costs 47.81 a day. Around how many such queries a day make the two cost the same?
hint: Divide the day of Redshift by the price of one query.

choices.text: About 27
choices.why: That divides by 1.8, ten times the price of a query.

choices.text: About 500
choices.why: At 500 Athena costs 90.00, nearly twice the workgroup.

choices.text: About 2,656
choices.why: That divides by 0.018, a tenth of the price of a query.

choices.text: About 266
choices.why: Right: 47.81 ÷ 0.18 = 265.6. Fewer than that, Athena; more, Redshift.

prompt: The lake's copy of an order and Aurora disagree about its total. Which is right?
hint: One store of record per fact.

choices.text: The lake, because it keeps every change DMS captured
choices.why: It is a copy derived from Aurora, and a copy that disagrees has missed something.

choices.text: Whichever was written most recently
choices.why: Recency is not the rule; the copy may be newer and still wrong.

choices.text: Aurora, the store of record
choices.why: Right; the lake's pipeline is what to investigate.

choices.text: Neither until a person decides
choices.why: The design already decided, by naming the store of record.

prompt: Which part of the 10.50 USD DynamoDB month for "my orders" is the largest?
hint: Look at the three lines of the table.

choices.text: The 3,000,000 reads
choices.why: They cost 0.56.

choices.text: Storage beyond the first 25 GB
choices.why: Right: 9.38 of the 10.50.

choices.text: The 600,000 writes
choices.why: They cost 0.56 too.

choices.text: The global secondary index on the date
choices.why: There is none: the date is the sort key.

prompt: If the screen were opened 1,000,000 times a month, each an Athena query billed at the 10 MB minimum, what is the least the scans cost, at 9.00 USD a terabyte?
hint: One million times 10 MB, in terabytes.

prompt: Quitanda's orders already live in an Aurora instance that has room to spare. What does adding "my orders" there, as one indexed query per lookup, add to the bill?
hint: What is Aurora's price made of?

choices.text: Another 338.25 a month, the price the section computed
choices.why: That is the price of an instance for this workload alone; the instance already exists.

choices.text: 10.50, the same as DynamoDB, since the requests are the same
choices.why: Aurora does not price per request; it prices the instance.

choices.text: Close to nothing; the machine is paid for
choices.why: Right; at most some I/O, which the table priced at a few dollars.

choices.text: The 270.00 minimum, as Athena would charge
choices.why: That is Athena's per-query minimum; Aurora has none.

prompt: Why does a busy `jobs` table used as a queue in PostgreSQL get slower over time?
hint: What does an update leave behind?

choices.text: PostgreSQL limits a table to a number of updates a day
choices.why: There is no such limit.

choices.text: `SKIP LOCKED` stops working past a thousand rows
choices.why: It works at any size; the problem is the dead rows around it.

choices.text: The workers' polling fills the write-ahead log
choices.why: Reads write no WAL; the updates do, and the bloat is in the table.

choices.text: Each finished job leaves a dead row, faster than vacuum cleans
choices.why: Right, and every poll then wades through them.

prompt: A DynamoDB table keyed by order id is asked for "the orders of customer c-17". With no index, what does that become?
hint: The key is not the customer.

choices.text: A `Query` on the customer, as fast as by the id
choices.why: A `Query` needs the partition key, which is the order id here.

choices.text: A `Scan` with a filter, reading and billing every item
choices.why: Right: the filter is applied after the read, so the whole table is paid for.

choices.text: An error until the table is recreated with a new key
choices.why: DynamoDB allows the scan; it just costs the whole table.

choices.text: A request DynamoDB answers from its cache of recent items
choices.why: There is no such cache for arbitrary attributes.

prompt: An application inserts an order into Redshift twice, with the same declared primary key. What does Redshift do?
hint: Declared is not enforced.

choices.text: Refuses the second insert with a key violation
choices.why: That is what a relational database that enforces keys does.

choices.text: Keeps the newer row and drops the older
choices.why: It keeps both; nothing merges them.

choices.text: Stores both rows
choices.why: Right: its keys are declared and not enforced, which is one reason an application's writes do not belong there.

choices.text: Queues the second insert until the first commits, then refuses it
choices.why: Commits do queue, and the second still goes in.

prompt: A query opens 500,000 small objects in S3. At 0.00056 USD per 1,000 GET requests, what does it pay in requests alone, in USD?
hint: 500 thousands.

prompt: Each of 800 delivery drivers sends a position every five seconds. The app shows each driver's latest position; the operations team wants a month of positions for route analysis. Which design fits both?
hint: Two access patterns: one key, now; and all of history.

choices.text: One Aurora table of every position, queried for the newest per driver
choices.why: Nearly 14 million rows a day on the business database, to answer a question about one row per driver.

choices.text: Newest point per person in DynamoDB; the stream to S3 for Athena
choices.why: Right: each access pattern on its own branch, the stream feeding both.

choices.text: Redshift for both, loaded every five seconds
choices.why: A warehouse loaded row by row is the third anti-pattern, and the app would wait seconds.

choices.text: One S3 object per position, read by the app for the newest
choices.why: Millions of tiny files, and the app listing them to find the latest.

prompt: Which of these are anti-patterns this lesson warns against? Choose all that apply.
hint: A store serving an access pattern it was not built for.

choices.text: A `jobs` table polled every second by workers
choices.why: Yes: a database as a queue.

choices.text: A DynamoDB table whose partition key is the order status
choices.why: Yes: few values, one hot partition.

choices.text: An application writing single rows into Redshift
choices.why: Yes: a warehouse as an application's store.

choices.text: Firehose buffering events into larger files in S3
choices.why: That is the cure for tiny files.

choices.text: ElastiCache in front of Aurora for the catalogue page
choices.why: That is the design of this lesson's workloads.

prompt: A new feature searches products by any words in their descriptions, ranked by relevance, as the customer types. What does the first question tell Quitanda?
hint: Is this access pattern on any branch of the tree?

choices.text: Use an Aurora `LIKE '%word%'` query, since products live there
choices.why: A leading wildcard uses no index and ranks nothing; it is the relational store bent to a pattern it does not serve.

choices.text: Scan the DynamoDB table with a `contains` filter
choices.why: The second anti-pattern, on every keystroke.

choices.text: Run an Athena query for each keystroke
choices.why: Seconds per answer and the 10 MB minimum per query.

choices.text: It is a pattern none of these stores is built for
choices.why: Right: full-text search wants a search engine, fed from the store of record, rather than bending one of these.
